guide.what: An interjection is a short word or phrase that shows a feeling or reaction (surprise, pain, joy) or does a social job (greeting, thanking). It stands alone, does not change form, and is usually written between exclamation or question marks.

rules.d: Spanish opens and closes exclamations and questions: ¡…! and ¿…?. If the interjection starts a longer sentence, the marks wrap only the exclamation part.
The most common way to react. «Qué» always has an accent here. To add a noun and adjective use «tan» or «más»: ¡Qué día tan bonito!
rules.exEn: What a pity! What a big house!

rules.d: «Cuánto» (with accent) agrees with the noun: cuánto, cuánta, cuántos, cuántas. Before a verb it means «how much».
rules.exEn: So many people! How much I missed you!

rules.d: «Ojalá» (I hope) is followed by the subjunctive, never the indicative. «Que» after it is optional. Same with «Dios quiera que…» and wishes with «¡Que…!».
rules.exEn: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow!

rules.d: Some interjections take «de» + a person to show pity or warning. It sounds dramatic or literary.
Formulas like ¡Buenos días!, ¡Disculpe! and ¡Con permiso! work everywhere. Slang like ¿Qué xopá?, ¡Ofi!, ¡Chuzo! or ¡De una! is only for friends. Never use slang in the DELE writing tasks.
rules.exEn: Excuse me, sir, can you help me?

rules.d: Some interjections come from verbs and change with tú or usted: ¡Oye! / ¡Oiga!, ¡Mira! / ¡Mire!, ¡Disculpa! / ¡Disculpe!, ¡Cuídate! / ¡Cuídese!.
rules.exEn: Excuse me, you dropped your wallet!

rules.t: Fillers for the DELE oral test
rules.d: Short fillers (bueno, pues, a ver, o sea, este) let you think without silence and sound natural. Use them to start answers or rephrase, but do not repeat the same one every sentence.
rules.ex: Bueno, a ver… pues creo que tiene razón.
rules.exEn: Well, let's see… I think he's right.

rules.d: Many interjections belong to one country: ¡Vale! (Spain), ¡Órale! (Mexico), ¡Che! (Argentina), ¿Qué xopá? (Panama). In Panama prefer ¡Dale!, ¡Listo! or ¡Claro! for «OK».

mistakes.why: Open the exclamation with ¡ and put the accent on «qué».
«A ver» (let's see) is two words; «haber» is a verb.
«Vale» sounds Spanish; Panamanians use dale, listo or claro.

items.use: The standard greeting at any time of day, with anyone. Often followed by another greeting: «¡Hola, buenos días!».
items.exEn: Hi! How are you?

items.use: Say it for any favor or service. Add «por» + noun or infinitive to say what for: «Gracias por venir».
items.exEn: Thanks for the help!

items.use: Shows you just understood or remembered something. Very common before «sí», «ya» or «claro».
items.exEn: Ah, now I get it! It's tomorrow.

items.use: The all-purpose cry for pain, fear, worry or surprise. Repeat it for drama: «¡Ay, ay, ay!».
items.exEn: Ouch! I burned myself with the coffee.
items.latam: Used everywhere; in Panama you hear it constantly.

items.use: Buys time, starts an answer, or closes a topic. In Mexico «¿Bueno?» is also how you answer the phone.
items.ex: Bueno, creo que es hora de irnos.
items.exEn: Well, I think it's time to go.
items.latam: Used everywhere; Mexico also uses «¿Bueno?» on the phone.

items.use: A friendly, strong «yes». Use it to accept a request or agree with an idea.
items.exEn: "Can you help me?" "Sure!"

items.use: Calls someone's attention, informally (tú). With «usted» say «¡Oiga!». Not rude if your tone is friendly.
items.exEn: Hey! Do you have a minute?
items.latam: Used everywhere; in Panama and Peru you also hear the short form «¡Oe!».

items.use: Draws attention to something you see, or introduces an explanation. Formal form: «¡Mire!».
items.exEn: Look, what a nice car!

items.use: Starts an answer or adds emphasis. «Pues sí» = well, yes. «Pues no» = well, no.
items.exEn: "Are you coming?" "Well, I don't know yet."
items.latam: Very common in Mexico and Spain; also used in Panama.

items.use: Use it after a small mistake, bumping someone, or to interrupt politely.
items.exEn: Sorry! I didn't see you.

items.use: Use it until about noon. Always plural: «buenos días», never «buen día» in most countries.
items.exEn: Good morning, ma'am! How did you wake up?
items.latam: Argentina and Uruguay often say «¡Buen día!».

items.use: Informal goodbye from Italian «ciao». Also written «chau» in the Southern Cone.
items.exEn: Bye! See you Monday.
items.latam: Very common in Panama and all of Latin America; Argentina writes «chau».

items.use: Asks someone to repeat, or adds «right?» at the end of a sentence. «¿Eh?» alone can sound abrupt; «¿Cómo?» is softer.
items.exEn: It's good, huh?

items.use: Means «I understand», «done» or «stop it», depending on the tone. «¡Ya, ya!» = OK, OK, calm down.
items.exEn: OK! I understood you.
items.latam: Used everywhere; Chile uses «ya» constantly for «OK».

items.en: OK! / Go ahead! / Let's do it!
items.use: Informal yes to a plan or a «go ahead». Also cheers someone on: «¡Dale, dale!».
items.exEn: "See you at eight?" "OK!"
items.latam: Very common in Panama, Colombia, Venezuela, the Caribbean and Argentina.

items.use: Stronger thanks. Never say «muchos gracias»: «gracias» is feminine.
items.exEn: Thank you very much for everything!

items.use: The standard reply to «gracias». Literally «of nothing».
items.exEn: "Thanks." "You're welcome!"
items.latam: Used everywhere; in Panama «¡A la orden!» and «¡Con gusto!» are just as common.

items.use: Used both as a greeting after dark and as goodbye before bed.
items.exEn: Good evening! Do you have a table for two?

items.use: From about noon until dark. In stores and offices, always greet with it before asking.
items.exEn: Good afternoon! I'm looking for the pharmacy.

items.use: Goes at the start or end of a request. Said alone with emphasis it can mean «Come on!»
items.exEn: A coffee, please.

items.use: Neutral goodbye. In the street people also say «adiós» quickly as a passing greeting.
items.exEn: Goodbye! Have a good day.
items.latam: Used everywhere; in Latin America «chao» is more common among friends.

items.use: Reacts to good news. Pattern ¡Qué + adverb!
items.exEn: They gave you the job? Great!

items.use: Means «done» or «agreed». Very useful to close a deal or a plan.
items.exEn: "I'll send it tomorrow." "OK!"
items.latam: Very common in Panama and Colombia for «OK, deal».

items.use: Cheers people on or urges them to move. «¡Vamos, tú puedes!» = come on, you can do it.
items.exEn: Come on, we're going to be late!

items.use: The typical Latin American thinking sound, like «um». Hold the final vowel: «esteee…».
items.ex: Este… no me acuerdo de su nombre.
items.exEn: Um… I don't remember his name.
items.latam: Very common in Panama, Mexico and all of Latin America; Spain prefers «eh…» or «pues…».

items.use: Use it while you think or check something. Written as two words: «a ver», not «haber».
items.ex: A ver… creo que la respuesta es la B.
items.exEn: Let's see… I think the answer is B.

items.use: Rephrases or explains what you just said. Overused by young people, so don't repeat it too much.
items.ex: No puedo ir, o sea, no tengo tiempo.
items.exEn: I can't go, I mean, I don't have time.

items.use: Common, polite goodbye, even if you won't see the person later today.
items.exEn: See you later! Thanks for everything.

items.use: Friendly goodbye. Add a time: «¡Nos vemos mañana!».
items.exEn: See you on Friday!

items.use: Small surprise, a near accident, or something a bit scary. Lighter than «¡Ay!».
items.ex: ¡Uy! Casi se me cae el vaso.
items.exEn: Whoa! I almost dropped the glass.

items.use: Simple surprise or admiration. Sounds a bit more formal or written than «¡Ah!» or «¡Uy!».
items.exEn: Oh! What a surprise to see you here!

items.use: Surprise, sometimes mild disappointment. «¡Vaya, qué pena!» = oh, what a shame.
items.exEn: Wow! I didn't know you spoke Chinese.
items.latam: Used everywhere; for Panama's «¡Vaya pues!» see that entry.

items.use: Reacts to surprising news. As a statement, «¡En serio!» means «I mean it!».
items.exEn: "I'm getting married in March." "Really?"

items.use: Reacts to good news. «¡Qué bueno que viniste!» uses «que» + verb.
items.exEn: So good that you arrived safely!

items.use: Say it before passing someone, leaving the table, or entering a room. The reply is «¡Propio!» or «¡Adelante!».
items.exEn: Excuse me, can I get by?
items.latam: Used everywhere; in Panama the short «¡Permiso!» is very common.

items.use: Polite (usted) way to get attention or apologize. Informal: «¡Disculpa!».
items.exEn: Excuse me! Where is the bathroom?

items.use: A real apology or sympathy. Stronger: «¡Lo siento mucho!».
items.ex: ¡Lo siento! Se me olvidó tu cumpleaños.
items.exEn: I'm sorry! I forgot your birthday.

items.use: Warns of danger. Add «con» for the danger: «¡Cuidado con el perro!».
items.exEn: Careful! The floor is wet.

items.use: Alone it means «I hope so». Before a verb it needs the subjunctive: «Ojalá que llueva».
items.exEn: I hope Panama wins the game!
items.latam: Used everywhere; the «que» after it is optional.

items.use: Strong surprise or worry. Very common and not offensive in Spanish.
items.exEn: Oh my God, what traffic!
items.latam: Used everywhere; Spain also says «¡Madre mía!».

items.use: Reacts to surprising news, good or bad. Literally «don't tell me».
items.exEn: "Ana won the lottery." "No way!"

items.use: Shows sadness or disappointment. With a verb use subjunctive: «¡Qué lástima que no vengas!».
items.exEn: You can't come? What a pity!

items.use: Means «what a shame». In much of Latin America it also means «how embarrassing».
items.exEn: I'm so embarrassed! I arrived late.
items.latam: In Panama, Colombia and Mexico «qué pena» often means embarrassment; in Spain only «what a shame».

items.use: Shows you are listening or agree. Also «aha!» when you discover something.
items.exEn: "And then you turn right." "Uh-huh."
items.latam: Used everywhere; very frequent in Panama and the Caribbean.

items.use: Strong agreement or praise: «exactly» or «well done». «¡Eso es!» means the same.
items.exEn: That's it! That's how you do it.

items.use: Total agreement. Also «¡Exactamente!».
items.exEn: "So it's tomorrow?" "Exactly!"

items.use: A clear yes, a bit more formal than «¡Claro!».
items.exEn: "Can I pay by card?" "Of course!"

items.use: Say it when you meet someone. The reply: «¡Igualmente!» or «¡El gusto es mío!».
items.exEn: Nice to meet you! My name is Carlos.

items.use: Two uses: a toast with drinks, and the reply when someone sneezes.
items.exEn: Cheers! To the bride and groom.
items.latam: Used everywhere; after a sneeze some people say «¡Jesús!».

items.use: Said to people who are eating, even strangers in a restaurant. Reply: «¡Gracias!» or «¡Igualmente!».
items.exEn: Enjoy your meal! Enjoy it.
items.latam: Very common in Panama and Latin America; Spain also says «¡Que aproveche!».

items.use: Congratulates on any good news or a birthday. Also «¡Felicitaciones!».
items.exEn: Congratulations on your graduation!
items.latam: Used everywhere; Spain also says «¡Enhorabuena!» for achievements.

items.use: Short, friendly greeting for any time of day. Common when entering a store.
items.exEn: Hi! Do you have cold water?
items.latam: Very common in Panama, Colombia and Costa Rica.

items.use: Casual greeting. Also «¿Qué tal + noun?»: «¿Qué tal el viaje?».
items.exEn: Hi, Marta! How's it going?

items.use: Food tastes great, or something feels pleasant (a cool breeze, a hot shower).
items.exEn: This sancocho is delicious!
items.latam: Used everywhere in Latin America; in Spain «rico» is mostly for food.

items.use: Pattern ¡Qué + adjective! The adjective changes: «¡Qué bonita!» for a feminine noun.
items.exEn: How lovely Casco Viejo is!

items.use: Relief after effort, or tiredness and heat. Also written «¡Uff!».
items.exEn: Phew! I finally finished the exam.

items.use: Strong shock or disbelief, often about bad news.
items.ex: ¡No puede ser! Perdí el celular otra vez.
items.exEn: It can't be! I lost my phone again.

items.use: Strongly denies or rejects what someone said. Informal.
items.exEn: "Are you tired?" "Not at all! I'm fine."
items.latam: Common in Spain, Cuba, Panama and the Caribbean.

items.use: Literally «eye». Warns or draws attention to an important detail. «¡Ojo con…!» = be careful with…
items.exEn: Careful! That bus doesn't stop here.

items.use: Warm reply to «gracias», or a yes to a request.
items.exEn: "Thanks for the ride." "My pleasure!"
items.latam: Very common in Panama, Costa Rica and Colombia.

items.use: Reply to «gracias», or what shop staff say to offer help.
items.exEn: "Thank you very much." "You're welcome!"
items.latam: Very Panamanian and Colombian; rare in Spain.

items.use: Returns a wish or a «nice to meet you».
items.exEn: "Have a good weekend!" "Same to you!"

items.use: Friendly goodbye (tú). With usted: «¡Cuídese!».
items.exEn: Bye, take good care!

items.en: Have a good one! / All the best!
items.use: Goodbye wish. «Que» + subjunctive. With usted: «¡Que le vaya bien!».
items.ex: ¡Que te vaya bien en la entrevista!
items.exEn: Good luck in the interview!

items.use: Short wish before an exam, game or trip. Stronger: «¡Mucha suerte!».
items.exEn: Good luck on the DELE!

items.use: Strong approval of a plan or news.
items.exEn: We're going to the beach Saturday? Awesome!

items.use: Agrees and confirms a plan. Very common in work and service situations.
items.exEn: "The appointment is at three." "Perfect!"

items.use: Informal praise for something nice or fun.
items.exEn: Your shirt is so cool!
items.latam: Very common in Panama, Colombia, Venezuela and Peru; Mexico says «¡Qué padre!», Spain «¡Qué guay!».

items.use: Relief that something bad didn't happen. Can add «que» + verb.
items.exEn: Thank goodness you brought an umbrella!

items.use: Encourages someone who is sad or facing something hard.
items.exEn: Cheer up! Tomorrow is another day.

items.use: Borrowed from English and very common in speech. The Spanish spelling «¡Guau!» also exists.
items.exEn: Wow! What a beautiful view.
items.latam: Very common in Panama and Latin America because of English influence.

items.use: The sound of laughing. In texts: «jaja» or «jajaja».
items.exEn: Ha ha! What a good joke.

items.use: Asks for silence. Also written «¡Chis!» or «¡Chist!».
items.exEn: Shh! The baby is asleep.

items.use: Added to plans for the future. Very common, not only among religious people.
items.ex: Nos vemos el lunes, si Dios quiere.
items.exEn: See you on Monday, God willing.
items.latam: Extremely common in Panama and Central America.

items.en: What a scare! / You scared me!
items.use: After a fright. Also «¡Me asustaste!».
items.ex: ¡Ay, qué susto! No te oí entrar.
items.exEn: Oh, what a scare! I didn't hear you come in.

items.use: Disgust at a smell, taste or sight.
items.exEn: Gross! This milk has gone bad.
items.latam: Used everywhere; Latin America says «dañada», Spain «estropeada».

items.use: A stronger, warmer «¡Claro!».
items.exEn: "Will you save me a seat?" "Absolutely!"

items.use: A strong no. Also answers «sorry» or «am I bothering you?».
items.exEn: "Am I bothering you?" "Not at all!"

items.en: Oh well! / Nothing to be done!
items.use: Accepts a situation you can't change.
items.ex: Se fue la luz. ¡Ni modo, cenamos con velas!
items.exEn: The power went out. Oh well, we'll eat by candlelight!
items.latam: Very common in Mexico and Central America; less so in Spain.

items.use: Mild surprise or annoyance. A polite word, safe in any company.
items.ex: ¡Caramba! Otra vez se me olvidó la llave.
items.exEn: Darn! I forgot the key again.
items.latam: Used everywhere; sounds a bit old-fashioned to young people.

items.use: Same as «¡Caramba!», shorter. Mild and polite.
items.exEn: Gosh, everything is so expensive!
items.latam: Common in Mexico and Latin America.

items.use: How you answer the phone in much of Latin America.
items.exEn: Hello? Who am I speaking with?
items.latam: Used in Panama, Colombia, Peru, Chile and Venezuela; Mexico says «¿Bueno?», Spain «¿Diga?».

items.use: Agrees with the person: «bienvenida» (woman), «bienvenidos» (group).
items.exEn: Welcome to Panama!

items.use: Pattern ¡Qué + noun! for fear.
items.ex: ¡Qué miedo! Ese puente se mueve mucho.
items.exEn: How scary! That bridge moves a lot.

items.use: Relief or gratitude. Very common in daily speech.
items.ex: ¡Gracias a Dios llegamos antes de la lluvia!
items.exEn: Thank God we arrived before the rain!
items.latam: Very common in Panama and Latin America.

items.use: A polite, warm yes. Not a negative, despite the «no».
items.exEn: "Could you pass me the salt?" "Of course!"
items.latam: Very common in Latin America; less used in Spain.

items.use: Small mistake or accident.
items.exEn: Oops! I dialed the wrong number.

items.use: Tells someone to stop. Stronger: «¡Ya basta!».
items.exEn: Enough! I don't want to argue anymore.

items.use: A warm goodbye or thanks, especially in messages.
items.exEn: Thanks for everything. Blessings!
items.latam: Extremely common in Panama and Central America, in person and on WhatsApp.

items.en: How annoying! / That makes me mad!
items.use: Anger or frustration. With a verb use subjunctive: «¡Qué rabia que…!».
items.ex: ¡Qué rabia! Perdí el bus por un minuto.
items.exEn: So annoying! I missed the bus by a minute.
items.latam: Used everywhere; Mexico also says «¡Qué coraje!».

items.use: Reacts to something terrible or very ugly.
items.ex: ¡Qué horror! Hubo un accidente en la autopista.
items.exEn: How awful! There was an accident on the highway.

items.use: Answers a question about the future with hope.
items.ex: —¿Crees que pases el examen? —¡Ojalá que sí!
items.exEn: "Do you think you'll pass the exam?" "I hope so!"

items.use: Goodbye when you'll see the person the next day.
items.exEn: See you tomorrow, teacher!

items.use: Applause or praise after a performance or achievement.
items.exEn: Bravo! You sang very well.

items.use: Celebration. «¡Viva + name!» cheers a person, team or country.
items.exEn: Long live Panama!
items.latam: Used everywhere; heard a lot on November patriotic holidays in Panama.

items.en: Give it your all! / Go for it!
items.use: Encourages effort. With usted: «¡Échele ganas!».
items.ex: ¡Échale ganas al estudio, que tú puedes!
items.exEn: Put effort into studying, you can do it!
items.latam: Very Mexican; also understood across Central America.

items.use: Simple encouragement before a challenge.
items.exEn: Come on, you can do it! You're almost there.

items.use: Invites someone to enter or to continue.
items.exEn: "May I come in?" "Come in!"

items.use: Short call for attention, or a warning. Can sound rough; use with friends.
items.exEn: Hey! Don't touch that.

items.use: Surprise at a near fall or slip, or a friendly greeting.
items.exEn: Whoa! Watch the step.
items.latam: Common in Panama, Venezuela, Colombia and the Caribbean.

items.en: Sure, right away! / Let's do it!
items.use: Informal, enthusiastic yes. Means «at once, without doubt».
items.exEn: "Shall we get some empanadas?" "Let's do it!"
items.latam: Very common in Panama, Colombia and Ecuador; not used in Spain.

items.use: Accepts a plan or closes a conversation, often before saying goodbye.
items.exEn: Alright then, see you tomorrow.
items.latam: Very Panamanian; also heard in El Salvador and Honduras.

items.use: Panama's classic informal greeting. «Xopá» is «pasó» with the syllables swapped. Only with friends.
items.exEn: What's up, bro? All good?

items.use: Surprise, shock or admiration. Informal but not offensive.
items.exEn: Wow! Is that car yours?

items.use: Surprise or amazement, good or bad. Informal.
items.exEn: Whoa, what a downpour!

items.use: Polite stand-in for a stronger word. Shows surprise or annoyance.
items.ex: ¡Chuleta! Se me quedó la cartera en la casa.
items.exEn: Darn! I left my wallet at home.
items.latam: Panama; a polite way to avoid a rude word.

items.use: Singular «diablo» shows strong surprise or emphasis. Informal.
items.exEn: Man, it's so hot today!

items.use: Short for «oficial». Confirms a plan or says «definitely». Young, informal.
items.exEn: "Are you going to the party?" "For sure!"

items.use: Joy and excitement, at parties, dancing or good news.
items.exEn: Woohoo! We won the game!
items.latam: Common in Panama, Puerto Rico and the Caribbean.

items.use: A stronger «¡Ayala!» for big surprise or dismay.
items.ex: ¡Ayala vida! Se me olvidó la reunión.
items.exEn: Good grief! I forgot the meeting.

items.use: Annoyance at something boring or irritating.
items.exEn: What a pain! There's a traffic jam again.

items.use: Shock at something excessive, unfair or terrible.
items.ex: ¡Qué barbaridad! Cobran veinte dólares por un café.
items.exEn: Good heavens! They charge twenty dollars for a coffee.

items.use: Strong surprise, either positive or negative; context decides.
items.exEn: Amazing! You finished the marathon.
items.latam: Very common in Argentina and Uruguay; also used in Panama.

items.use: Relief after worry.
items.exEn: What a relief! I found my passport.

items.use: Joy at good news or seeing someone. With a verb: «¡Qué alegría verte!».
items.ex: ¡Qué alegría verte después de tanto tiempo!
items.exEn: I'm so happy to see you after so long!

items.en: No way! / Out of the question!
items.use: A firm no. In some countries it can also mean «oh well».
items.exEn: Lend him my car? No way!

items.use: Literally «lie!», but usually means «I can't believe it», not an accusation.
items.exEn: "I got the scholarship." "No way! Congratulations!"
items.latam: Very common in Latin America as friendly disbelief.

items.use: Calls someone quietly. Can be rude with strangers; use with friends.
items.exEn: Psst! Come here a moment.
items.latam: Used everywhere; in Panama people also hiss «¡Chist!».

items.use: Disappointment or worry at bad news.
items.exEn: Oh no! It started to rain.

items.use: Wish for someone who is sick. «Que» + subjunctive. With usted: «¡Que se mejore!».
items.exEn: Get well soon!

items.use: Said to someone who is traveling.
items.exEn: Have a good trip! Let me know when you arrive.

items.use: The standard birthday wish.
items.exEn: Happy birthday, Mom!

items.use: Cry for help in danger.
items.exEn: Help! Someone is drowning!

items.use: Same as «¡Socorro!», a bit more common in Latin America.
items.exEn: Help! Call the police!
items.latam: Used everywhere; very common in Latin America.

items.use: Mild frustration. Polite, a bit like cartoon language.
items.exEn: Shoot! My battery died.
items.latam: Used in Latin America, often heard in dubbed cartoons.

items.use: Frustration or surprise. Mild, but avoid it in formal settings.
items.exEn: Darn! I lost my keys.

items.use: Disgust at a taste or smell. Also «¡Puaf!».
items.exEn: Yuck! This soup is too salty.

items.use: Strong disgust. Informal and a bit childish.
items.ex: ¡Guácala! Hay una cucaracha en el piso.
items.exEn: Gross! There's a cockroach on the floor.
items.latam: Common in Mexico, Central America, Panama and Colombia.

items.use: Disgust, often about a smell. Informal, used a lot with kids.
items.exEn: Pee-yew! What smells so bad?

items.use: Shows you don't care or don't believe something.
items.exEn: Bah! That's not important.

items.use: Hopes something bad won't happen.
items.exEn: "Do you think it'll rain?" "I hope not!"

items.use: Like «ojalá». Before a verb it needs the subjunctive: «Dios quiera que…».
items.exEn: God willing, everything will go well!
items.latam: Common in Panama and Latin America.

items.use: Interjection + «de» + person. Dramatic, a bit literary or joking.
items.ex: ¡Ay de mí! Tengo tres exámenes mañana.
items.exEn: Poor me! I have three exams tomorrow.
items.latam: Used everywhere, mostly joking or in literature.

items.use: Sympathy. It agrees: «¡Pobrecita!», «¡Pobrecitos!».
items.exEn: Poor thing! He fell off his bike.

items.use: Sound of a hit, a fall or an explosion. Also used in stories for something sudden.
items.ex: Y de repente, ¡pum!, se fue la luz.
items.exEn: And suddenly, boom!, the power went out.

items.use: The sound of a sneeze. The usual reply is «¡Salud!».
items.exEn: "Achoo!" "Bless you!" "Thanks."

items.use: Shows that food is tasty, or that you are thinking.
items.ex: ¡Mmm! Qué rico huele ese arroz con pollo.
items.exEn: Mmm! That chicken and rice smells delicious.

items.use: Very Mexican: agreement, surprise or encouragement, depending on tone.
items.exEn: "See you at five." "OK!"

items.use: Surprise or worry about a problem.
items.exEn: Oh boy! I didn't bring any money.
items.latam: Mexico and parts of Central America.

items.use: Informal warning, literally «waters».
items.exEn: Watch out! A car is coming.
items.latam: Mexico only; in Panama say «¡Cuidado!» or «¡Ojo!».

items.use: The standard «OK» in Spain. Learners hear it in Spanish textbooks and DELE audios.
items.exEn: "I'll call you later." "OK!"
items.latam: Spain. In Panama and Latin America say «¡Dale!», «¡Listo!» or «¡Okey!».

items.use: Encourages or agrees, from «venir».
items.exEn: Come on, you can do it!

items.use: Calls attention to a friend.
items.exEn: Hey, come here a second!

items.use: Costa Rica's famous phrase for «great», «thanks» or «hi».
items.exEn: "How are you?" "All good!"
items.latam: Costa Rica; Panamanians know it well from their neighbors.

items.use: Praises a person or a situation as nice and fun.
items.exEn: Your boss is so nice!

items.use: Celebration, a bit old-fashioned or childish.
items.exEn: Hooray! No school tomorrow.

items.use: Sound of a quick hit, or something that happens suddenly.
items.exEn: And, wham!, the door slammed shut.

items.use: The sound of a kiss, often at the end of messages to family and friends.
items.exEn: I love you lots, mwah!

items.use: Sound of knocking on a door; also starts jokes.
items.exEn: Knock, knock! May I come in?

items.use: Old-fashioned surprise. You meet it in books, cartoons and dubbing.
items.exEn: Good heavens! How late it is!
items.latam: Used everywhere, mostly in books and dubbed TV.
